new_statements.rule_in_words: Numana is transcribed and described as a tone language: for the Ningye dialect Blench reports three level tones plus glides (tentatively); for Numana proper (Aza/Gbantu area) Blench's own wordlist marks high, low, unmarked (mid), rising and falling tones on lexical items but leaves the '3.3 Tones' section blank. No source says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be stated.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the tone statement is explicitly tentative ('still to be analysed'), and tone-raising is named as a plural-formation device (§4.1, §4.3 empty table)
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms in a one-shot 348-item wordlist; nothing about phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted tone statement is about the Ningye dialect (Glottolog ning1271, ex-ISO [nns], merged into Numana [nbr] by ISO change request 2018-090 in 2019; Ningye speakers call themselves Numana). Blench's Numana wordlist proper (Aza village, Gbantu/Janda area) is tone-marked but its Tones section is blank. Blench's 'Numbu' 2006 file is a verbatim duplicate of the Numana file, not separate Numbu data. Nunku (Blench 2006 Nunku wordlist) is being reassigned to Mada [mda] and was not used.

sources.note: Section 3 Phonology (printed p. 2): 'The phonology of Numana is based on rapid observations and should therefore be regarded as tentative'; 3.1 seven vowels, 3.2 consonant chart, 3.3 Tones = heading only with NO text. Wordlist forms carry tone diacritics (grave, acute, unmarked, caron, circumflex: Àzà Wúùn, mgbyǎn/mgbyán, mkpàŋ/mkpáŋ). a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prominen|pitch|syllab returns nothing.
